item.title: Cascading impacts of Atlantic meridional overturning circulation weakening and collapse on marine biogeochemistry
item.dc:creator: Paul E. Lerner, Anastasia Romanou
item.description:
Communications Earth & Environment — matched: Arctic, tipping point, bifurcation, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, Earth system model, Earth system, ensemble
Abstract As anthropogenic emissions continue to increase Earth’s surface temperature, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is at risk of weakening substantially and crossing a tipping point. Then, multiple Earth system components may be significantly and irreversibly altered. Here we investigate the responses of ocean carbon uptake, net primary productivity (NPP), oxygen concentration, and carbon storage to an AMOC collapse induced by extremes in the internal variability in the subpolar gyre under a moderate forcing scenario. While similar ensemble splitting has been found in other models, the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) Earth system model (ESM) was the first to report an AMOC bifurcation due to internal variability, without the need to prescribe freshwater hosing. We find severe regional impacts, including collapsed NPP and deoxygenation in the subpolar North Atlantic, and reduced carbon uptake in the Arctic and subtropical North Atlantic. We identify the physical drivers of these ocean biogeochemical impacts and, for the first time, provide estimates of their lag and latency, i.e. the timescales over which these impacts begin to occur and are fully realized, respectively. Timescales are generally found to increase southward from the deep convection sites, but are remarkably similar between basins at similar latitudes.

item.title: Persistent bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters over 800,000 years
item.dc:creator: Nathan Stevenard, Aline Govin, Catherine Kissel, Didier Swingedouw, Samuel Toucanne, Nathaëlle Bouttes
item.description:
Science Advances — matched: hysteresis, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, interglacial, millennial-scale, sediment core, sea level
The stability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major uncertainty in projections of future climate. However, direct evidence for AMOC tipping behavior on orbital timescales remains scarce. Here, we reconstruct the strength of Iceland-Scotland Overflow Water, a key lower branch of the deep Atlantic circulation, over the past 800,000 years by combining 12 current-speed records from North Atlantic sediment cores with a data-driven hybrid model. The resulting reconstruction reveals persistent alternation between weak (glacial) and strong (interglacial) circulation modes, pervasive millennial-scale variability within both regimes, and systematic asymmetry between weak-to-strong recoveries and strong-to-weak collapses. Threshold and phase-space analyses show that regime shifts occur within a narrow window of atmospheric carbon dioxide and sea level and often follow hysteresis-like loops. Although bistability persists throughout the last 800,000 years, its sensitivity and timing evolve through time. These findings provide long-term, high-resolution, data-driven constraints on the bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters and its implications for AMOC resilience in a warming world.

item.title: Regional Arboreal Pollen Input and Its Millennial-Scale Variability Recorded in an Alpine Lake in the Hengduan Mountains, China
item.dc:creator: Jing Wu, 昌迪 柯, Yi Huang, Hongwei Meng, Lingyang Kong, Min Wang, … (+2)
item.description:
Biology — matched: millennial-scale, Holocene, ensemble
The Hengduan Mountains are a major hotspot for lake-sediment research, but regional vegetation responses to Holocene climate variability remain incompletely understood. Here, we analyzed pollen assemblages and concentrations from Dinggongniang Co (4633 m a.s.l.) to investigate regional vegetation-related changes over the past approximately 4.7 ka. Pollen percentage and concentration analyses were combined with ensemble empirical mode decomposition (EEMD) and Lomb–Scargle spectral analysis. Despite being located above the modern tree line, the lake sediments are dominated by arboreal pollen (89.5%), particularly Pinus, indicating substantial pollen input from lower-elevation forests. Total pollen concentrations were relatively low around 4.2 ka, increased markedly during the Roman Warm Period, and remained relatively elevated during the Medieval Climate Anomaly, suggesting changes in regional arboreal pollen input potentially associated with Asian summer monsoon-related hydroclimatic variability. Furthermore, time-series analyses identified a possible millennial-scale oscillation at approximately 1.3–1.4 ka, broadly consistent with variability documented in North Atlantic and Asian monsoon records. This finding highlights the value of high-altitude lake pollen records for tracing regional arboreal pollen input and suggests possible connections between Asian monsoon variability and broader Northern Hemisphere climate fluctuations. Although chronological uncertainties and multiple factors influencing pollen concentrations introduce some limitations, the observed patterns offer valuable insights into long-term vegetation-related environmental variability in the Hengduan Mountains.

item.title: A Deep-Learning Framework for the Generalized Emulation of Atmospheric Radiative Transfer at Microwave Frequencies
item.dc:creator: Spencer R. Jones, Simon Pfreundschuh, Christian D. Kummerow
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: sea ice, emulator, machine learning, neural network
arXiv:2611.07094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents an application of machine learning to the problem of the computational expense of atmospheric radiative transfer calculations from physics-based models. While in recent studies individual emulators have been created that emulate certain radiative transfer schemes for different sensors, we show that a general framework can be applied to emulate the radiative transfer method itself. A fully connected deep neural network has been trained to predict top-of-atmosphere microwave radiances in all-sky conditions over various land, ocean and sea ice surfaces at all frequencies from 1 to 300 GHz, and for all incidence angles from 0 to 65 degrees. The reference models against which the emulator has been trained include an Eddington two-stream radiative transfer model for one-dimensional and pseudo-three-dimensional microwave brightness temperature simulations. This neural network architecture has also been separately trained to reproduce the explicit calculations of the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) for a single microwave imager. In all cases, the model architecture is successfully able predict microwave brightness temperatures by being trained directly on the optical properties of the atmosphere and surface and therefore directly emulating the radiative transfer method. Compared to the explicit schemes used to produce the training data, the GPU-enabled emulator is able to produce brightness temperature simulations more than three orders of magnitude faster and with a root-mean-squared-error less than 0.0348 K, 0.0531 K, and 0.0246 K against the independent test data for the two Eddington models and CRTM, respectively. Additionally, preliminary training using a full 3D Monte Carlo scheme for high-resolution simulations shows promising results for the application of this method to "exact" radiative transfer methods, and these results are discussed in Section IV.

item.title: Explainable AI for Geoscientific Regression: Evaluating Sensitivity and Attribution Methods with the Lorenz-63 System and Applications
item.dc:creator: Ieuan Higgs, Todd Jones, Kieran Hunt, Anna-Louise Ellis
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: dynamical system, Earth system, emulator
arXiv:2608.07406v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) moves from research prototypes to operational tools in Earth system science, trust in its predictions becomes increasingly important. Explainable AI (XAI) offers insight into how AI models make predictions. However, many influential XAI methods were developed or popularised for classification, and their interpretation for regression, which dominates geoscience, is less well established. A central obstacle is the lack of ground truth for judging explanations. We show that, for a dynamical system with known governing equations, matched references can be built directly from the physics. We extend established sensitivity methods to provide physical references for both sensitivity and attribution, separately for methods with implicit and explicit baselines, all computed from the governing equations independently of the network. Applied to an AI emulator of the Lorenz-63 system, these references show that method families answer distinct questions rather than approximating one ``true'' explanation. The emulator's sensitivities and attributions can depart most from their physical references where it forecasts best, so predictive skill is not a substitute for the physical realism of what a model has learned. We then review XAI applications to Earth system regression, organised by method family, extending to issues an idealised system cannot address: computational scalability, strongly correlated high-dimensional predictors, and reliance on expert judgement where no physical reference exists. We also discuss how an XAI method can be mathematically valid yet only partially relevant to a given stakeholder group. We close with future directions and practical recommendations for responsible XAI use in geoscientific modelling and forecasting.

item.title: Impact of temperature variability on mortality during extreme heat and cold conditions over 20 years: A time-space-stratified case-crossover study
item.dc:creator: Yuchen Wei, Fang Guo, Yawen Wang, Zihao Guo, Guozhang Lin, Conglu Li, … (+5)
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: heat extreme, climate change
by Yuchen Wei, Fang Guo, Yawen Wang, Zihao Guo, Guozhang Lin, Conglu Li, Shi Zhao, Chao Ren, Kin Fai Ho, Eng Kiong Yeoh, Ka Chun Chong Background Climate change-induced temperature variability poses growing health risks. The effects of this variability on mortality are well established; however, its specific impact during extreme heat and cold conditions remains understudied. This represents a knowledge gap, as the human body’s physiological capacity to adapt to sudden temperature shifts is compromised when ambient temperatures are extreme. To address this, our study examined the relationship between mortality and temperature variability in Hong Kong for a 21-year period. Methods A time-space-stratified case-crossover design was used in this study. Daily weather data from ERA5-Land and PM2.5 levels from ChinaHighPM2.5 were combined with mortality records in Hong Kong from 2000 to 2020. Diurnal temperature range (DTR) and temperature changes between consecutive days (TCN) were used as the temperature variability metrics. Extreme hot and cold conditions were defined by annual temperature percentiles: > 75%, > 90%, > 95%, > 97.5% for hot seasons, and Results DTR and TCN were strongly associated with mortality during heat extremes. For temperatures >97.5th percentile, DTR (odds ratio [OR] = 1.99, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.90-2.08) and TCN (OR = 2.24, 95% CI: 2.09-2.40) showed increased risks for all-cause mortality. During cold extremes ( Conclusion Temperature variability was associated with an increased risk of mortality during extreme heat conditions, with mortality risk rising alongside higher extreme temperature levels, while during extreme cold, the associations were generally smaller. At temperatures above the 97.5th percentile, each 1°C increase in DTR and TCN was associated with approximately 99% and 124% higher odds of all-cause mortality, respectively. These findings highlight the need for targeted public health strategies to protect vulnerable populations from climate-induced temperature fluctuations.

item.title: Detecting Weather Fronts from Satellite Observations: What Does Reanalysis Add?
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Dravilas, Miruna Stoicescu, Roope Tervo, Carlos Horn, Oriol Hinojo Comellas, Sina Montazeri, … (+2)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: reanalysis, machine learning
arXiv:2611.08148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weather fronts are transition regions between air masses with contrasting thermodynamic properties and are associated with mid-latitude precipitation and severe weather. We investigate machine learning (ML) methods for detecting weather fronts and quantify the contribution of reanalysis data to performance. We compare two configurations of the same ML model for pixel-wise frontal classification over the North Atlantic and Europe: (1) using only geostationary infrared satellite observations, and (2) additionally using 28 ERA5 reanalysis fields. The satellite-only model achieves a neighbourhood critical success index at a 150 km tolerance (CSI@150) of $0.402$, which lies within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services. The satellite$+$ERA5 model achieves $0.575$, an improvement of $0.173$. Our analysis shows that low-level winds are the least predictable from the satellite representation ($R^2 = 0.23$, compared with $0.88$ for temperature), while removing winds or moisture causes the largest decreases in detection performance.

item.title: Antecedent Snowpack Conditions and Shifting Hydroclimatic Controls on Vegetation Productivity: Implications for Sustainable Watershed Management
item.dc:creator: Yuru Yan, Wei Xu, Pai Liu
item.description:
Sustainability — matched: snowpack, climate change
Climate warming is altering seasonal snow regimes and vegetation phenology in cold regions, but the influence of snowmelt may extend well beyond spring thaw. We examined how snow-related associations with net primary productivity (NPP) changed across the growing season in the Naoli River Basin during 2014–2024. Monthly NPP was reconstructed using the Carnegie–Ames–Stanford Approach and evaluated against MODIS NPP. The growing season was divided into early (EGS), peak (PGS), and late (LGS) stages based on vegetation phenology. Generalized additive models identified contemporaneous, lagged, and cumulative associations of air temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, and snow water equivalent (SWE), while random forest and partial dependence analyses were used to compare driver importance and SWE–NPP responses. SWE showed antecedent associations, with AIC-selected April-referenced windows A0L4 (EGS; R2 = 0.23) and A0L3 (LGS; R2 = 0.24). Solar radiation remained the most important predictor, but its relative importance declined from 53.77% in the EGS to 42.56% in the LGS. SWE was more important than precipitation in the EGS (18.96% vs. 12.38%) and PGS (17.31% vs. 13.86%), whereas precipitation became more important in the LGS (19.75% vs. 15.13%). The SWE–NPP relationship also shifted from an overall declining response in the EGS to a nonlinear response in the PGS and a predominantly positive response in the LGS. These results highlight the value of considering antecedent snowpack conditions alongside growing-season climate in vegetation productivity monitoring, with implications for sustainable watershed management under climate change.

item.title: Estimating ensemble-mean anomaly correlations and the ratio of predictable components using an unbiased estimate of the predictable signal variance
item.dc:creator: Christopher David Roberts
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: ensemble
arXiv:2611.07878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The correlation ($r$) between ensemble mean forecasts and observations is a frequently-used metric of forecast quality in the weather and climate prediction communities. However, uncorrected estimates of $r$ are biased towards zero at finite ensemble size due to the influence of unpredictable noise that contaminates the sample ensemble mean. This note summarises established ensemble-size adjustment methods and characterises the behaviour of $r_{\infty}$, a correlation estimator that is constructed from an unbiased and ensemble-size-independent estimate of the signal variance. The only requirement is that forecast members are exchangeable with one another such that they can be interpreted as independent draws from a case-specific predictive distribution. The estimator $r_{\infty}$ does not require forecasts and observations to be statistically exchangeable, only that the unpredictable component of each member is uncorrelated with the observed truth, and thus works for both reliable and unreliable forecasts. In some situations, $r_{\infty}$ may be undefined (i.e. the estimated signal variance is negative) or fall outside the admissible range $-1 \leq r_{\infty} \leq 1$ when the predictable signal is small relative to the sampling uncertainty. These inadmissible values can be interpreted as evidence that the true predictable signal cannot be resolved with the available ensemble size and number of cases. The same unbiased signal variance can also be used to estimate the correlation between the predictable signal and individual members to yield an ensemble-size-invariant estimator of the ratio of predictable components (RPC). In contrast, variance-based RPC estimates, including forms that correct only the model predictable component, are biased low by a factor that depends only on the ensemble size and model signal-to-noise ratio.

item.title: A Land-Sea Contrast Pattern in Surface Temperature and Atmospheric Circulation Trends in Recent Decades
item.dc:creator: Benjamin O. Johnson, Maria Rugenstein
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: sea level, CO2
arXiv:2606.19581v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We argue land-sea contrast is an important driver of spatial patterns of observed surface temperature and atmospheric circulation trends, including the negative Inter-Decadal Pacific Oscillation (IPO)-like tendency across the Pacific basin. Observed and modeled trends display an overall decline in sea level pressure over the faster-warming land, with a spatial pattern that resembles the seasonal cycle and modeled response to land heating. Coupled historical forcing climate model simulations underestimate the land-sea warming ratio. It is only in the early response of abrupt CO2 quadrupling climate model simulations that climate models are able to recreate the observed land-sea warming ratio, in which case a negative IPO-like sea level pressure trend and surface warming pattern over the Pacific comparable to observed trends are seen. We propose that some discrepancies between observed trends and those predicted by climate models are explained by the underestimation of the land-sea warming ratio by climate models.

item.title: Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya
item.dc:creator: Ashim Sattar, Shashi Kant Rai, Abhinav Alangadan, Adam Emmer, Sunil Dhar, Umesh K. Haritashya, … (+1)
item.category: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
item.description:
Natural hazards and earth system sciences — matched: glacier, meltwater
Abstract. The Warwan sub-basin in Jammu and Kashmir is a remote glaciated region containing several glacial lakes and has recently experienced population growth and infrastructure development. Due to inaccessibility and geomorphic masking, multiple mass movement events including avalanches and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) have remained largely unreported. This study analyzes three major avalanche events from the past two decades. The September 2005 and September 2020 avalanches originated from glaciers GL-B and GL-A within the same glacier complex, while the March 2020 rock–ice avalanche initiated from the headwall of glacier GL-F in an adjacent valley and terminated before reaching its ablation zone. Runout mapping shows that the September 2020 avalanche descended from the headwall of GL-A and impacted its proglacial lake, triggering a GLOF. In contrast, the September 2005 event terminated before reaching the glacial lake that began forming in 1999 at the terminus of GL-B. Geomorphic analysis indicates persistent sediment influx from meltwater streams of GL-D and GL-E into the lake associated with GL-A, progressively infilling the basin. Continued glacier retreat caused meltwater to accumulate behind the sediment infill, dividing the basin into two disconnected lakes. Impact from the September 2020 avalanche led to complete drainage of stored water and sediment, generating a downstream debris flow. Pre- and post-GLOF imagery reveals breaching and widening of the outflow channel and deposition of a debris fan downstream. The repeated history of mass movements and continued growth of glacial lakes raise serious hazard concerns in the Warwan sub-basin. GLOF modeling identifies Lake-B as potentially hazardous lake at the present condition posing significant downstream risk. Settlements such as Youdu and Qaderna, along with bridges, roads, and residential structures, lie within potential GLOF inundation zones. High sediment availability from past mobilization and deposition along the valley increases the potential of debris flow cascades, posing elevated risks to downstream infrastructure and hydropower, underscoring the need for preparedness and mitigation planning. GLOF modeling suggest that early warning system closer to the source will be able to provide a good lead time in case of potential GLOFs in the valley.

item.title: Linking the evolution of floe sizes to the sea-ice deformation history using SAR imagery
item.dc:creator: Nils Hutter, Cecilia M. Bitz
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: polar
Polar oceans are covered by many pieces of floating ice, called floes, that vary in size, shape and thickness. This study focuses on how fracturing caused by stresses from wind and ocean currents changes floe sizes. Using satellite images, we track ice motion and floe sizes, and study floe shapes and how deformation alters the distribution of floe sizes. We find that stronger deformation creates more small floes and present a formula to include this effect in sea-ice models.
